 STEVENSVILLE — He's always had a love for the game.Tim Goodrich played his high school football at Chesapeake High in Anne Arundel County. Years later he ran Kent Island's youth program, where he met former Kent Island High head coach Bryon Sofinowski.
Goodrich got into coaching to be with his sons, and eventually got involved with Kent Island High's program. There he developed into one of the Bayside Conference's more respected defensive coordinators, coaching under Sofinowski, Damian Ferragamo, Sofinowski again, and last year Zach Davis.
"I don't know why, but I'm still here," Goodrich joked earlier this week.
The why this year is because Kent Island needed a head coach, when Davis stepped down after one season to take an administrative position in Queen Anne's County. Goodrich agreed to fill the vacancy on an interim basis this season, and makes his head coaching debut Friday, when the Bucs open their season at Cambridge-South Dorchester.
"Other than a lot more paper work and questions it's not much different," Goodrich said, comparing the head coach and defensive coordinator roles. "We have a great supporting staff. All of our guys have pretty much been here before so I've got help everywhere. I have a great team-Mom system set up and they take of a lot of pressure off me. The administration's been great. It's just a little more time and some more stuff other than football. To this point, it's been relatively smooth."
Goodrich hopes it stays that way, but knows facing Cambridge-SD, Middletown and Easton to start the season may have its share of bumps.
"Excited and nervous," Goodrich said of opening the season. "When I stop being nervous is when I stop coaching, right? But I feel good where we are."
Among the reasons for feeling good is a defense that returns eight from last year. The front line features senior Jeremiah Bounds (6-foot-3, 227 pounds) at end, junior Zach Bunce (6-5, 245) and senior John Guy (6-0, 230) at tackle, and senior Gerson Chevez (5-9, 235) at nose guard. The linebacking group again looks strong, with seniors Jaxson Hess (5-10, 202) and Savion Keene (6-0, 180) playing outside, and senior Kerry O'Brien (5-10, 205) teaming with junior Mason Guy (5-10, 185) inside.
"We've got experience, and they know what we expect and what we do as a defense," said Goodrich, who also returns seniors Andy Bennett (6-2, 175) and Scooter Wright (5-9, 160) at the corners, while senior Luke Umstot (6-1, 173) is at safety. "I would say our defense is probably a little ahead of our offense right now."
Part of that may be attributed to the preseason-long battle at quarterback between junior Trace Klapaska (6-0, 188) and senior Ryan Brestensky (5-10, 157), who have each shined at times in scrimmages. Whoever gets the starting nod will have the usual blue-collar, ground-and-pound backfield behind him, led by Hess, O'Brien and sophomore Alex Brestensky (5-8, 150).
Keene and Umstot start at wide receiver.
"We have the pieces to be successful," Goodrich said of his offensive.
The biggest of those pieces are up front. Senior John Guy (6-0, 230) and Bunce start at the tackles. Seniors Greg Coffey (6-4, 298) and Mike Luttrell (6-2, 265) are at guard, bookending Queen Anne's transfer Mac Windsor (5-10, 225) at center. And Bounds is at tight end.
"Maybe there's been two years in my time here that we've had an offensive line as big as we have this year," said Goodrich, who enters his 20th year with the program. "We're actually gigantic all the way across the offensive line. We should be able to move people. And that's what we do anyway."

 CAMBRIDGE — Rob Burnham created one tough act to follow."I am keenly aware of that," Burnham said with a slight laugh.
Burnham's also aware he has no one to blame but himself, his staff and his players. In just his first year as Cambridge-South Dorchester High's head football coach, Burnham piloted the Vikings to their first undefeated regular season since 2000, when David Bromwell — then in his first year as head coach — led his alma mater to a perfect 10-0 regular-season. Though the 2024 Vikings played one less regular-season game than the 2000 edition, both teams finished with 10-1 records.
So what's Burnham's plan for an encore on the eve of his second season?
"The goal is to win more than 10. It always has been," said Burnham, whose team's unbeaten run ended last year via a Class 1A state quarterfinal loss to eventual state champion Fort Hill.
Though Anthony Hughes, the two-way standout who was selected as last year's Bayside Conference Most Valuable Player, has graduated, Cambridge-SD again looks to have the goods for another successful season and deep postseason push.
Sophomore Nate Twilley (5-foot-10, 190 pounds) takes over at quarterback and has a trio of talented running backs behind him, including 5-8, 175-pound senior Sterling Perkins, who rushed for over 1,000 yards a year ago. He is joined by classmates Jayden Hollowell (5-9, 160) and Ra'Quan Cornish (5-10, 150), who like Perkins, have big-play potential.
"We're going to rely on our run game," Burnham said. "And we're going to throw it enough to keep people honest, keeping them from loading the box."
Twilley has a talented fleet of senior receivers to aim for, as Majestic Jones (6-0, 170), Tamyron Evans (5-8, 150), Leonbre Chester (6-1, 170) and TJ Wilson (6-3, 180) have the potential to take any catch they make to the house. Complementing that cast are three tight ends, led by senior K'Marion Hall (6-3, 225), who may be the most talented player on the roster.
"I can play him anywhere," Burnham said of Hall. "He can play all five offensive line spots. He can play tight end. He can play receiver, wing and fullback. He can do pretty much everything."
Senior Russell Johnson (6-1, 215) and junior Parker Spies (5-11, 195) are also at tight end and join a young offensive line.
Returning from last year are junior right guard Jeffrey Sellman (6-0, 250) and junior Tellorian Williams (6-6, 245), who shifts from center to left tackle. Junior Christian Reynolds (6-1, 225) starts at center, with sophomore Amori York (6-1, 295) at left guard and junior Donnell Bryant (6-3, 235) lining up at right tackle.
"We're young," Burnham said of his line. "We don't have any seniors on the line so we're trying to catch up. I know coach (Tim) Goodrich and the Kent Island Buccaneers, when they come to town (Friday) they're going to have a good game plan. We're going to have to be ready for them, and we're going to have to grow up in a hurry on that offensive line so we can be ready, hopefully have success against those guys."
The defense figures to again be tough and flock to the ball quickly.
"We pride ourself on running fast to the football, striking it and driving it backwards," Burnham said. "That's how we coach defense, and that's the expectation."
Senior Zion Pinder (6-1, 250) and Johnson start at the tackles, flanking sophomore nose guard Reggie Parker Jr. (5-11, 275). Hollowell and Spies are at inside linebacker. Hall is at one outside linebacking spot and will be joined by either senior Steven Marine (5-10, 150) or Paxton Adkins (6-0, 160). Jones and Cornish return at the corners, with Evans at one safety and sophomore Tyion Parker (6-0, 160) at the other.
"We have some of that big-play potential that we had before," Burnham said. "We have a consistency in our run game, and we've shown growth over the course of the last couple weeks. We've gotten better each day. We're almost there. We got a chance to be at the level we expect to be at really really soon, but we're going to have to continue to improve. And hopefully we can get more than 10 (wins). That's our goal."

author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton looking to go deep

 September 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 EASTON — The 2023 high school football season wasn't the best of times for Easton High.Starting wide receiver Chase Raab was lost before the preseason. Quarterback Mikey O'Connor suffered a season-ending injury in Week 2. That injury list eventually ballooned to seven offensive starters, not exactly a recipe for a deep postseason run.
So head coach Matt Griffith inserted his younger players, hoping they would gain the experience needed to help the Warriors turn things around in 2024.
And what a turnaround it was.
All Easton did last season was go from a 1-8 in 2023 to 8-4, the biggest about-face in the program's past 40 years. That turnaround included a pair of playoff victories, the first time the Warriors had done anything like that in at least 40 years.
"We had a good year," said Griffith, who finished with the highest win total in his 10 years at the helm, and earned his 50th career victory when Easton defeated Kent Island in the second round of the Class 2A East Regional playoffs.
Now, Griffith and company want more.
"We're not going to rest on what we did last year," said Griffith, whose team joins Kent Island and Queen Anne's in the move from Class 2A to the 2A-1A ranks this season. "And while that was a successful season for some, we're going to choose success (based on) playing in the first week of December. If you're not going into the season thinking you want to play in the state championship game, then you got to change your mindset. We want to be better than we were last year."
Easton graduated seven seniors from last year, including O'Connor — now at Merrimack (Mass.) College — but return 17.
For the first time since 2018, an O'Connor will not start the season at quarterback for Easton. Brady Walls, a 6-foot-4, 210-pound junior who backed up Mikey O'Connor last season, takes control of an offense that looks solid at every spot.
"Size. Strong arm. High IQ," Griffith said of Walls. "He's a competitor. So he's going to put us in a good place. He's done a good job so far managing the offense in the preseason, and we're looking forward to hopefully a big junior year from him."
Griffith is also hoping to get some big games from his backfield, led by senior Dustin Blue (5-10, 212), sophomore Jamiere Copper (5-9, 200) and junior Jordan Horsey (5-11, 210).
"Physical, downhill runners," Griffith said. "We relied a lot on the running game last year with Mikey and a combination of the running backs. I think the running backs will take more of the running load this year. That's not saying Brady won't (run). But Brady won't run as much as Mikey did."
When Walls does drop back, he'll be looking at a receiving cast that has the potential to be among the Bayside Conference's best.
Lining up at wideout will be a combination of seniors Carter Mooney (6-0, 180) and Kent Island transfer Isaiah Diaz (6-4, 185), and freshmen Nicky O'Connor (6-1, 185) and Tatum Brooks (6-1, 180). There's also plenty of talent at slot, with seniors Zach Barnhart (5-8, 195), Kyree Acree (6-0, 175), sophomore Chad Stanley (6-0, 175) and Horsey.
"Isaiah, Nicky, Tatum and Chad are new to the system," Griffith said. "They're learning it. I think they are going to continue to get better as the year goes on. The more time we have for Brady to throw the ball and go through his progressions, the better off we'll be."
Providing that time for Walls and the holes for the backs is a seasoned group, led by three seniors — left tackle Tymiere Thomas (5-11, 275), center Jack Chapple (6-3, 225) and right guard TJ Truxson (5-11, 305). Junior Xavier Stowers (6-3, 240) returns from last year and starts at right tackle, while sophomore Brady Gilliece (6-4, 275) is at left guard. Junior Darrien Downes (6-2, 270) will be rotated in plenty.
"I think we're pretty happy with where we're at so far," Griffith said of his line. "We still have a lot of work to do. Great group. So they all return from last year, and Darrien is a nice addition to that starting core."
The defense also looks solid, returning nine of 11 starters from last year — it would have been 10 of 11 had senior Dionte Copper not suffered a season-ending injury over the summer.
Thomas and Stowers are at tackle, while senior Jeremiah Stanley (6-2, 185) and junior Messiah Joseph (5-9, 185) rotate at nose guard. Senior Tracey Groce (5-11, 285), juniors Elias Leonard (6-0, 315) and Braiden Fluharty (6-3, 225) provide depth up front along with Downes and Gilliece.
"Second year in the system with last year being the first in a new system under Al (Waters)," Griffith said of his defensive coordinator. "I think we're able to play a little faster. It's less teaching and learning, and more scheme and technique."
Linebacking could be a strength, with Jamiere Copper and Horsey starting inside, and senior Tayshaun Roberts (5-9, 215) and Blue setting up outside. Senior Alex Rhodes (5-10, 205) will get time inside, and juniors Teddy Antal (6-1, 185) and Nevin Whitaker (5-10, 215) figure to get snaps outside.
The secondary has senior Logan Friend (5-9, 165) and Brooks at the corners, though Diaz will also play there. Chad Stanley and Acree are at free safety, with Barnhart, Mooney and junior Jerrell Flanagan (5-10, 170) roaming at strong safety.
"I expect our defense is what kind of carries us early while our offense is still starting to click a little," Griffith said.
Seniors Kai Ferrias and Luke Stanco share the place-kicking duties, while Griffith can use either Axel Spalin or Horsey to punt.
"The Bayside's a tough conference to play in, and we're going to be challenged every week," Griffith said. "If our kids continue to do what we're asking them to do, and expecting them to do, we'll be able to compete with pretty much anybody that we play."

Tue looking to lay a foundation

 WORTON — Paul Tue feared the rumblings Kent County High may not field a football team this season were teetering on the edge of becoming a sad reality as summer pushed into August."There were rumors all up and down the Shore," Tue said. "We didn't know we were going to have a program until two weeks before the season."
A former assistant, Tue said Harold Somerville stepped down as Trojans head coach after three years upon receiving a recent job promotion. Tue submitted an application for the vacancy, got the nod as the new head coach, and now begins a rebuilding project with what may be the Bayside Conference's youngest — and smallest in terms of numbers — varsity roster.
"We're basically resetting the program, trying to establish a culture of discipline and accountability from years past," Tue said.
The handful of talented reinforcements that made their first practice Tuesday has the potential to help that process.
Scottie Ford, a 6-foot, 160-pound senior and wrestling standout, returns at fullback and linebacker. Junior Dwan Harris (6-2, 225), who started at quarterback last year, could again line up behind center and also plays defensive end. Senior track star RJ Peterson (5-11, 155) and junior newcomer Micah Handy (5-6, 128) bolster the receiving corps and secondary. And junior Dylan Hurtt (5-11, 150) is at the slot, while freshman Joe Gonce (5-11, 240) figures to see time on the offensive and defensive lines.
The bulk of that group injects some much-needed experience, but won't be eligible to play until Week 2 at Arcadia (Virginia).
As for now, Tue takes over a program that will have no junior varsity this season. The offense heads into Friday's season opener at Bohemia Manor with four freshmen and three sophomores projected to start. The defense is set to start four sophomores and one freshmen. And nine of the offensive starters are slated to also start on defense.
"We have a lot of teaching to do," Tue said. "We have some players that have never played before since they were way younger. But we're not going to use age as an excuse for too long."
Having coached in Kent's youth program, Tue is familiar with a number of players on his roster. He's also familiar with the fact as he begins his first heading coaching post at the high school level, he and his staff will have to be patient with such a young team.
Zavion Brown, a 6-foot, 180-pound senior who played tight end last year, starts at quarterback, and is accompanied in the backfield by senior running back Rahzir Wilson (5-9, 150). The wide receiving fleet is young with junior Thomas Moore (6-1, 163), sophomore Xavier Johnson (5-4, 140) and freshman Wayne Brown (5-4, 117).
Providing time for Zavion Brown is the conference's youngest offensive line, that starts three freshmen — left tackle Finn Beiker (6-2, 255), center Daniel Poore (5-4, 156), and tight end Alijah Floyd (5-7, 180) — two sophomores — right guard Hunter Hawn (5-7, 190) and right tackle Dozie Okakpu (6-3, 270) — and senior left guard Jalen Rochester (5-11, 240).
While Tue has plenty to figure out offensively, his bigger concern may be defensively.
"We have to get a physicality about us," Tue said. "And it's hard to simulate in practice because you're worried about getting kids hurt because the numbers are so low. But me and my staff, we got to figure out a way to get some physicality out of these boys. That was the glaring weakness from the scrimmage; we didn't look too interested in putting a hat on somebody. That can't happen."
Again, youth and a lack of depth figures to limit what Kent can do defensively.
The defensive front has Moore and Hawn at the ends, Rochester and Okakpu starting at the tackles, and sophomore nose guard Jordan Turner-Henry (5-10, 247). Zavion Brown is at middle linebacker with Floyd on one side of him and senior Eli Wilson (6-0, 164) on the other. Wayne Brown and Johnson are at the corners with Wilson playing safety.
Moore will also handle the kicking chores.
Tue was encouraged by what he saw in Kent's only scrimmage against Rising Sun. The Trojans yielded a touchdown on the opening kickoff and fumbled to set up the Tigers' other first-half score, but otherwise held their own.
"I was happy with the first half," Tue said of an eventual 29-8 loss. "They competed.
"We won two games last year," Tue added. "I want to get to that and then I want to get past it."

title: Wilkins not throwing around great expectations
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Wilkins not throwing around great expectations

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 RIDGELY — Heath Wilkins may have been surprised last October when he was promoted to head varsity football coach at North Caroline High after Nic McMorris was let go halfway through his second season at the helm.What surprised Wilkins even more though was his team's resilience.
"Last year I was very surprised the team didn't fall apart," Wilkins said. "They wanted to keep playing. When I pulled them together when I first got the position, I was like, 'So, what are your expectations here?' They were like, 'Win it out. Going to the playoffs. Take the state championship.' I was like, 'OK.' I mean we still had (Stephen) Decatur on the schedule, but they were ready to go."
Wilkins' debut as varsity head coach ended with a 27-21 loss to James M. Bennett — the Bulldogs' narrowest margin of defeat to that point in 2024. After getting routed by Decatur a week later, Caroline lost by two at Kent Island and defeated county rival Colonel Richardson before getting routed in the first round of the Class 2A playoffs by Decatur, which went on to win a second straight Class 2A state championship.
So what are the expectations for the Bulldogs this season? None really, as far as their win-loss record is concerned.
"To be better than last year," Wilkins said. "No, I haven't told these guys we're going to go out and win every game. Literally I put the schedule on the (locker room) board and I got a question mark after every team. What are we going to do? We're going to have to take this game by game. I cannot throw expectations out there with the (1-9) record that we had last year. So we're set to take them one at a time."
North Caroline is also set to have one — if not the — biggest offensive lines in the Bayside Conference. Grayson Martin, a 6-foot-1, 255-pound senior, starts at center. Sophomore Tavon Townson (6-3, 365) is at right guard while junior Demarcus Forsith (6-6, 310) is next to him at tackle. The left side features junior Conner Hinson (6-1, 205) at guard and senior Wyatt Eaton (6-1, 220) at tackle. Sophomore Adam Deck (6-5, 230) is at tight end.
"We've got some size up front, but we do have some speed," Wilkins said.
There is also size and speed in the backfield.
If Caroline's scrimmage last Friday against Bohemia Manor was an indicator of things to come, senior fullback Caden Deavers could prove to be a 5-10, 226-pound sledgehammer, with or without the ball. Joining him are senior tailback Owen Walstrum (6-0, 180), senior wingback Owen Feltz (6-0, 230), and junior quarterback Tatelli Keihl (6-0, 170). Senior Glothier Gabriel (5-10, 165) returns at wide receiver.
But Wilkins admitted getting the team back to the Wing-T style of play he used on the junior varsity level has taken time.
"The seniors, I had them their freshman and sophomore years," Wilkins said. "The system changed (under McMorris). I'm just getting them reacquainted with it. It takes time to put in and to get it right. I want them to understand the concept as opposed to just having a job to do.
"It's been rough, getting them to buy in; getting them to trust and believe," Wilkins continued. "It'll come around."
Though Wilkins said his defense is a bit behind the offense in terms of preparation, he thinks that too will come around. He looks to have the personnel, with Forsith and Townson at the tackles, and some combination of Feltz, Eaton and Hinson at end. Junior Tray Lapor (5-9, 180) and senior David Kusyk (5-8, 205) are slated to start at inside linebacker, while Walstrum, senior Jaden Hall (5-10, 170) and junior Stephen Jones (5-10, 180) rotate at outside linebacker.
Manning the corners are senior Cole Compton (5-10, 175) and Gabriel, while Keihl starts at free safety.
"It's coming together slow," said Wilkins, who also returns place-kicker Mason Shilling. "I keep having to remind myself we're only two weeks into official camp. We had mini-camps. And of course my expectations are we should be able to go out and play a game tomorrow. But we're not ready to play a full-fledged game tomorrow. It's going to take time."
While Easton, Kent Island and Queen Anne's dropped to the Class 2A-1A East Region this season, North Caroline remains in the 2A East with Parkside and Wicomico. Two-time defending 2A state champion Stephen Decatur moved to the 3A South Region along with James M. Bennett.

 CENTREVILLE — Brian Mooney brimmed with optimism his first two years as Queen Anne's County High's head football coach.As he enters this season, Mooney admits, "This is the happiest I've been in my three years (as head coach)."
Perhaps the biggest reason for Mooney's sunny outlook is the Lions' collective team speed. Of course, anyone seeking a second opinion on that topic can ask Donny Graef, who was Queen Anne's head coach for 25 years and is now in his second year back as an assistant.
"It's not the fastest," Graef said. "But it's definitely one of the fastest teams."
Pacing the fast cast is 5-foot-9, 165-pound junior Jadereon Thompson, who starts at wide reciever and safety, returns punts and kickoffs, and can go from zero to the end zone practically every time he touches the ball. He has plenty of fast company that includes senior running back DeRodney Smith (6-0, 170), along with senior Carter Dickey (5-8, 150) and sophomore Zavione Sudler (5-7, 145), who can spell Smith when needed.
"Jadereon's a burner," Mooney said. "So is DeRodney. Zay can go, and Carter Dickey's really fast."
The group behind them aren't exactly slouches in the 40. The McDonald twins, Alex and Alan — both listed at 5-5, 140, are at wide receiver, though Alex could see time at running back. The receiving group also includes senior Brooks Blodgett (6-1, 175) and junior Chance Hegedus (6-2, 185). Senior Dorrin Phillips (5-9, 215) returns at fullback with junior Hunter Kelly (5-10, 195) behind him.
Mooney said he will make a decision over the weekend on his starting quarterback, which has been a battle between senior Lance Arnold (5-11, 185) and sophomore Colton Starlings (6-3, 190).
If it can stay healthy, the offensive line could also be a strength. Senior Drew Sutton (5-11, 235) returns at center. Lining up on the right side are a pair of classmates, guard Brian Maleski (5-11, 210) and tackle Gannon Brown (6-4, 215). Senior left guard Levi Frank (6-0, 160) saw time as a starter last season and is flanked by sophomore tackle Austin Mattei (6-3, 215). Senior Jamison Woodward (5-10, 180) starts at tight end.
"Hopefully we don't have to have as many combinations as we did last year," Mooney said of an offensive line that was plagued with injury from start to finish last season. "They're growing. Austin is still learning. But if we can just stay healthy it should be a good group.
"Every one's bought into what we're doing," Mooney continued. "So everybody has bought into their role. The typical things that you're kind of coaching all the time we're not having to go back and do all the time. This group is locked in. This group is special."
There is plenty of speed and grit on the defense as well.
Frank and Phillips start at end with senior Ryan Robinson (5-11, 175) and junior Khalil Lively (6-0, 180) being rotated into the mix. Sutton returns at tackle and is joined up front by junior Brayden Combs (5-11, 220), with Brown and Mattei in the rotation.
Maleski starts at inside linebacker and is paired with Kelly, who was moved up from strong safety. Woodward is behind them.
The secondary has the potential to be very good, with Thompson, Smith, Dickey and senior Wyatt Wilhoit (5-9, 180) at the safeties, and Blodgett, Hegedus, Alan McDonald and senior Elijah Billups (5-9, 150) at the corners.
The special teams could also be among the Bayside Conference's best with Thompson, Smith, Hegedus and Sudler handling punts and kickoffs. Junior Adrian Altamirano has shown a big leg in practice and could have a big impact.
Mooney was encouraged by what he saw during last Friday's scrimmage against a bigger St. Paul's team. But like a year ago, the Lions are thin and hope to avoid the string of injuries that hampered last season.
"Last year we felt really good going into the season and then had a couple of bumps with health," Mooney said. "That's always the key for everybody. But I think the sky's the limit. I don't see any reason why this team can't go deep in the playoffs."
Queen Anne's will be part of the 2A/1A East Region this season along with Southern (Anne Arundel), Calvert, Lackey, Hammond and fellow Bayside Conference rivals Easton and Kent Island.
"We're just going to take it one game at a time," Mooney said. "I know that's coach-speak, but that's kind of how we have to be right now because of where we are in terms of numbers. We just got to re-evaluate where we're at every week and keep rolling. It's just an exciting time."

 AMERICAN CORNER — There is experience and talent at the skill positions.As for the offensive line?
Well, Colonel Richardson High head football coach James Jackson knows there's little experience up front, but hopes with a lot of patience the talent gradually develops.
"They just have to be patient with the younger guys on the offensive line," Jackson said of his backfield. "The offensive line, basically everybody is new. So they have to be willing to work with these guys, run behind them this year. It's not going to start off smooth. It's going to take time. They've got to let everything build up."
There were times during last Thursday's practice when senior running back Derrick Mitchell and junior wingback Ja'Zir Dickerson blazed around end for big gains. There were other times when Jackson and longtime assistant Neil Lambert said, "Hold up," and walked their young linemen through their assignments.
"We graduated 16 from last year, including the entire starting offensive line," Jackson said of a team that went 6-5.
The right side of the line appears somewhat set with 5-foot-9, 270-pound freshman Andrew Baker at center, sophomore Dominique Rosado (5-9, 225) at guard, and senior Christian Cephas (6-6, 320) at tackle. There are battles on the left side. Junior Keke Donne (6-0, 225) and sophomore Dave Pierre are vying for the left guard spot, while sophomore Ethan Thomas (5-7, 160) and freshman James Jackson Jr. (5-9, 200) bid for the starting job at tackle.
"They're not afraid to ask questions, and I expressed that to them early," Coach Jackson said of his young line. "'We've got to ask questions. If you don't understand something, ask questions. Just don't go out and say you understand something and then get out there and mess up. It's better for you to ask questions, to make sure you're right than to go out there and mess it up. Because with our (double-wing T) offense, one missed block, one mistake can cost us yards. As long as you ask questions and continue to pick up details and progress, we'll be all right.'"
If the o-line develops as hoped, Colonel could be in position for its fifth winning record in Jackson's six years as head coach. Mitchell (6-0, 180) and Dickerson (6-1, 175) have plenty of speed and big-play potential. Senior Bradley Thomas (5-10, 205), who moves from wingback to starting quarterback, and senior fullback Chatydrick Pickrom (5-11, 230) add a physical dimension to the run game.
"Skill-wise, those guys are already up to par," Jackson said of his backfield. "They know what they should be doing. They know their expectations."
The expectation is for Colonel to again ground and pound the ball, though when he does throw, Bradley Thomas' main targets figure to be senior wide receivers Zyaaron Nichols (5-8, 150) and Jayquan Wilkins (5-6, 135), along with senior tight end Jordan Poole (5-10, 150).
Jackson doesn't think patience will be a must defensively since several players saw significant time a year ago. Ethan Thomas starts at right defensive end while Pickrom returns at left end. Senior Carlens Jean-Baptiste (5-6, 155) is at one tackle, while junior Kellio Dorleans (6-0, 180) and Cephas look to earn the starting nod at the other tackle.
Bradley Thomas anchors an inside linebacking unit that includes junior Jared Morales (5-11, 190) and freshman Jalen Epps (5-8, 205). Starting at outside linebacker are the Alexander twins, Evan (5-5, 145) and Anthony (5-7, 160) — who are juniors — though Poole could also see time.
Manning the corners are Wilkins, who led the team in interceptions last year, and sophomore Davonyae Childs (5-6, 135). Dickerson starts at safety.
"I don't think we have to be as patient with these guys because a lot of these guys have played in our system," Jackson said of the defense. "They just got to take the reps they got last year and build off of it."
Senior soccer player Jackson Jean handles the kicking duties, though sophomore Betsaleel Pierre kicks in games Jean can't attend.
"The more this group learns the higher the expectations become," Jackson said. "We hope they continue to keep building a tradition in the direction that Colonel football has been going."

 Queen Anne's County High School's Nicholas "Cole" Coppage delivered a national title performance under pressure, outlasting a field of more than 1,800 of the country's top high school shooters to win the 2025 USA High School Clay Target League National Championship on July 13, in Mason, Michigan.Coppage narrowly advanced to the final day, finishing Saturday's qualifying round with a score of 96 — good for 395th place and just inside the 400-athlete cut. But on Sunday, the junior shot a perfect 100-straight in the championship round and joined a 21-athlete shoot-off of fellow perfect scorers. Coppage then hit 45 consecutive targets in three tiebreaker rounds to clinch the title.
"Cole shot 240 consecutive targets on Sunday — and didn't miss once," said Head Coach Nathan Powell of the Queen Anne's County High School Clay Target Team.
"Through three grueling rounds of increasing difficulty, Cole maintained a laser focus and held his form through physical and mental fatigue, and earned himself the title of national champion. We have made a profound statement within the shooting sports world, that QACHS is an elite program and is a force to be reckoned with," he said
Coppage, who also helped anchor his team's 22nd-place national finish in the squad competition, rose to the top among more than 53,000 student-athletes who participated in the League this spring.
In the women's competition, Brianna Helsene of South Prairie High School (North Dakota) earned the national crown following a shoot-off with Aubree Antrim of Stewardson-Strasburg High School (Illinois).

Powell praised the entire squad's dedication throughout the season, which began with tryouts in March.

 Maddie Porter didn't have to be a vocal leader her junior year."I had three seniors that were kind of in that role," North Caroline High head softball coach Lee Hutchison said of his 2024 team. "This year she (Porter) took on that leadership role. She got the girls together preseason. She worked with a lot of the younger girls, getting them up to speed. So she took that leadership role on."
Porter also continued to be one of the Bayside Conference's toughest outs, batting over .500 for a second consecutive season while helping North Caroline stay in contention for the North Bayside title until the regular season's final weeks. That combination, along with some hefty offensive numbers, earned Porter the All-North Bayside's Player of the Year honor as selected by the division's coaches.
"Maddie was a great player, but she was never that authority," Hutchison said of his senior third baseman, who is headed to Arcadia (Pa.) University to play. "She was never one to push other players. And I don't know what happened, but this year it happened.
"They did some preseason hitting and stuff," Hutchison added of Porter and her teammates. "And she was calling players. 'Hey, you need to be hitting. You need to be doing this.' She was calling our young pitching and saying, 'Hey, you need to be throwing.' That was a big step for her."
Porter continued to be one of the conference's biggest hitters as well. The senior's .538 batting average led the Bulldogs and was second on the all-North first team only to North Dorchester' Jewels Vroman (.595). Hutchison's decision to move Porter from leadoff to third in the lineup proved to be a wise one, as she finished the year with 34 hits, 22 RBIs, five doubles, three triples and 25 runs. That move also had North Caroline (9-9 overall, 5-3 North Bayside) bidding for the North crown, as it handed North Dorchester its lone division loss before late-season losses to Kent Island and Easton ended Bulldog hopes.
"Her junior year she had so many hits and she got on base so many times in the leadoff, which was great because we had girls behind her that could drive her in," Hutchison said. "This year we felt that we had somebody (hitting leadoff) that could get on as much as her. Now, we needed somebody in that three hole that could drive in some runs, and that's why she ended up with more RBIs than she had (as a junior)."
Like Hutchison, North Dorchester head coach Carol Hubbard was hoping Vroman would step into more of a leadership role this season after the Eagles graduated some of their big-time leaders, including pitching ace Emilee Cohee and catcher Maggie Hubbard.
"I kind of hoped that she would," Coach Hubbard said of Vroman. "I didn't really know what to expect. We did lose a lot of leadership and big personalities with my seniors. But she (Vroman) definitely stepped up in all aspects of her game this year, both as far as leading by example by what she did in the (batter's) box and on the mound, and during the offseason.
"But also, she was a lot more vocal this year," Hubbard added. "She did a good job of motivating the younger players and keeping energy up in the dugout."
Vroman also did a good job replacing Cohee in the circle, compiling a 10-4 record that included a 1.10 earned-run average, 162 strikeouts and only 16 walks, earning the coaches nod as all-North Pitcher of the Year.
The junior left-hander helped the Eagles (17-5) clinch their third straight North Bayside title May 1, when she crafted her fourth no-hitter of the season while blanking Colonel Richardson. Five days later, Vroman tossed a two-hitter while leading North Dorchester to its first conference title via a 7-1 victory over eventual Class 2A state finalist Stephen Decatur.
The Eagles' season ended when they lost to eventual Class 1A state champion Mardela in the 1A East Region II final.
Vroman also impressed at the plate, batting .596 while leading the team in hits (44), home runs (three), RBIs (43), doubles (13) and triples (three).
"She's been a part of the team since we won the (1A) states her freshman year," Hubbard said. "She kind of looked up to the girls that were older than her and realized now, 'Hey, I'm one of the older girls that people are looking up to and I need to step into that role and step it up. And I really think she did."
Ryan Brice stepped into the role of Easton's head coach in 2024 and for the second consecutive season he and assistants Tracy Roe and Casey Baynard were named staff of the year.
"I feel they just need someone to believe in them, and we believed in them from day one," said Brice, whose team finished 13-6. "We told the girls, 'If you guys do x, y, z then we'll basically compete with anybody in the Bayside and the state. Once we're locked in it's going to be very tough to beat us.'"
Despite a bumpy stretch where they lost three of four games in early to mid-April — which included key division losses to Colonel Richardson and North Dorchester — the Warriors recovered, winning seven of their final nine games — the last a 3-0 loss in the 2A East II final to Stephen Decatur, which went on to reach the state final.
"We had a small blip in the road," Brice said of the rocky April patch when Easton was minus one of its starters. "But like I told all the girls, 'Every single one of those girls are on the team for a reason. And if we're not together as a unit then we're just basically off.'"
Once the Warriors had their full complement of players "we got back to a regular-scheduled program," Brice said. "And at the end of the day the result was competing for a regional championship. I told the girls, 'If we just stay together, we play together and work together, the sky's the lime for us.'"

 CHESTERTOWN — Due to the dock collapse at the Washington College boathouse during Tea Party weekend (May 23–25), the Maryland Special Olympics Kayaking Championship could not be held in Kent County as in previous years.While the event moved to Crisfield, the Kent County team hosted its own local competition Saturday, giving athletes a chance to paddle 150- or 500-meter races and celebrate their achievements.
Traveling to Crisfield was not feasible for all athletes.
"Traveling two-and-a-half hours was not convenient for some of the athletes," Coach Jenny Lee Freebery said.
Despite fewer competitors, the day was full of enthusiasm and achievement. Awards were handed out, and the event concluded with a special lunch honoring the athletes. Head coaches Freebery and 1972 Olympian Jack Brosius, assistant coaches Danielle Cudone and Anne Scott, as well as Ricky Freebery and parents, helped run the event.
Opening ceremonies began at the Washington College boathouse with Kent paddlers. Scott Kuster played "The Star-Spangled Banner" on his baritone horn, followed by the Pledge of Allegiance from newcomer Thos Stevenson. Brian Tate recited the athletes' oath before the competitions began.
Athletes adjusted to conditions after being unable to use the docks. Freebery, the only coach allowed on the dock, provided a recap of the racing. Competitors included McKenzie Weaver (150 meters, first season kayaking in a tandem with Cudone), Nick Gaorfal (150), Thos Stevenson (150, tandem with support staff Courtney Phelps), Woody Glenn Jr. (500, tandem with his father Woody Glenn Sr.), Chris Dooley (500), Tom Rickloff (500), Brian Tate (500), Robin Baker (500), and Scott Kuster (500).
Team members who did not compete this year due to schedule conflicts included Allison Bedell, Andrew Jackson, and Palmer Hopwood.
Freebery praised the athletes' dedication despite a challenging season.
"I'm so proud of our team. This year had a lot of challenges; the dock broke right before our season started, so we weren't able to use the beach for many practices. Then we had so many days with heat indexes over 100 degrees or thunderstorms on the horizon that kept us off the water," she said.
On Saturday, the paddlers persevered, showing determination and teamwork.
"Everyone put in such great effort and was very adaptable. It was rewarding watching our new paddlers go from never having been in a kayak before to racing down the Chester," Freebery said.
She also highlighted the camaraderie among athletes.
"Practices are always fun, with the athletes cheering each other on, helping carry boats, and pushing one another to do their best," she said.
The team hopes to host the Maryland championships again next year and is seeking more volunteers and Special Olympics paddlers for next summer. They also launched a campaign to acquire new boats and paddles. To support their cause, visit support.somd.org/team/755145.
Brian Tate, reflecting on the team's spirit, offered a possible motto:
"Teamwork makes the dream work," he said.

Governor's Cup race returns to St. Mary's College

 Sailors of all types and experience levels will hope they are on even keels and that they have fair winds this weekend as they take part in the 52nd annual Governor's Cup sailing race.The St. Mary's College of Maryland tradition, which is the oldest overnight race on the Chesapeake Bay, features a 68.6 nautical mile race from Annapolis to the college.
There are also two other satellite races, each of which is about 48 miles in length.
"I'm always excited for the Governor's Cup to return," said Race Director Rick Loheed, who is also the St. Mary's College associate director of the waterfront.
Boats departed Annapolis beginning 3 p.m. Friday and, depending on winds and other variables, are scheduled to arrive at the college early Saturday morning.
"There's something special about sailing back to the college you graduated from," said Michael Woolen of Baltimore, who graduated from St. Mary's College in 2014 and has taken part in the race about five times. "And there's something special about sailing overnight, assuming the conditions are advantageous."
Other options include the Potomac leg, which runs from Dahlgren, Va., to the college.
"They will sail to a marker at the mouth of the Potomac where the river is widest and then come all around to the 'SM' marker," Loheed said, adding that heading up the St. Mary's River is "a completely different challenge than sailing down the bay."
There is also a Solomons leg which has three entries this year.
"The Annapolis [leg] is more challenging because of the bigger distance and more water," Loheed said, "but they're all challenging and you're sailing at night."
There are 81 boats competing this year, which Loheed said "is on par with post-pandemic years."
Loheed will be pulling double duty as he will be sailing in his third Governor's Cup aboard his 35-foot Poor Richard, which will depart from Annapolis and compete in the CRCA Class.
"The more crew you have, the more righting movement you can have because they can all sit on the rail," Loheed said. "Many of these boats have heavy weighted keels. But by adding weight to the windward rail you help the righting moment of the boat fight against the sails trying to tip it over, so you're able to use a little more of that sail power to propel you forward a little faster."
Crew members will serve as bow, main trimmer, jib trimmer, helmsman and sewer guy, which is so named because they pack up spinnakers down in the cabin. Loheed will be the tactician.
"It's a challenging, grueling race," Loheed said. "A lot of times those faster boats overtake us and sometimes that happens during the day, but it also happens at night. The whole race is a challenge. You're constantly watching the Automated Identification System for other boats and as you go down the bay you have to make sure you're aware of the ships. They are much faster than most people realize."
He said the secret to having a successful race is "don't make any mistakes."
Woollen, who is planning on competing in the Annapolis leg aboard Jester in the PRFA Class, said that "most of the time sailing the rhumb line (the shortest point between A and B) is the fastest way in my experience. I think only one year has that not been the winning recipe."
For more information on the race, visit smcm.edu/signature-events/governors-cup-yacht-race/.

After several anxious moments, Springer slowly lifted his head. He mouthed the word "Wow!" before walking to the dugout with aid from a man on each side.
Whew.

 WESTON, WI — 12-year-old bowler Abigail Ticknor of Millington stays in her lane, then dominates in it. Even if that lane is at a national championship youth bowling tournament held in Northeast, Wisconsin.On July 14-19, she was the first ever bowler from Kent County to compete at the USBC Junior Gold Championships, an annual bowling tournament for the top male and female youth bowlers in the United States.
The competition was fierce and Ticknor, according to WBAY, a local news source in that area, competed against the top 3100 bowlers in the nation for nearly half a million dollars in scholarship prizes and a chance to be on the Junior Team USA.
She did not get to be one of the top 16 to go to the finals, but Ticknor placed 51rst in the nation in a field of 107 U12 girls at the 2025 edition of Junior Gold Championships.
Ticknor finished her 16 qualifying rounds with a total score of 2,222 for an average of 138.88, roughly a pin better than her league average from this past season.
Junior Gold, her father Phil Ticknor said is a challenging event, consisting of four four-game qualifying rounds, then an advancer and final rounds on a different sport-shot oil pattern each round.
"Sport-shot patterns force bowlers to make adjustments to how they usually bowl and each pattern plays differently," Phil pointed out, being present and cheering his daughter on.
Ticknor began qualifying play with a 493 (142-111-113-125) four-game round at Ashwaubenon on July 14, which put her in 85th place.
The next day, she moved up to 61th, after a 555 (122-156-134-143) at Dale's Weston Lanes in Weston.
Then at Ashwaubenon for round 3 she moved her up to 49th place before settling into 51rst with a 528 (143-103-127-155) at Dale's on July 17th.
Phil said, the highlight for Ticknor at the tournament came the night of July 16th when she opened her four-game qualifying round at Ashwaubenon.
"Those were two of the best games of her life on any type of oil pattern," Phil remarked.
Ticknor opened the evening with a five-strike, three-spare performance en route to a 177 game. In game two she topped that, opening with a turkey (three consecutive strikes) and finishing with five strikes and three spares, this time putting a 190 on the board. That score tied her highest-ever game on a sport-shot pattern and tied her fifth-highest ever score on any lane condition.
After bowling a 126 in game three, she finished the night strong with a 155 in the fourth and final game. Her total score in the round was 648 (162 average), giving her by far her best-ever single-day sport-shot performance.
Phil was thrilled with her very first performance on the national stage.
"I went in thinking her being in the 70s or 80s would have been a great success for it being her first time and where she is as a bowler — making top half was great!"
Ticknor had earlier earned her spot at Milford Bowling Lanes on Sept. 22 finishing third place in a co-ed field of a dozen U12 boys and girls in the first Delaware-sanctioned Junior Gold Qualifier of the season.
She bowls in the varsity division of the Doverama Dragons Youth League in Dover, Delaware.
Competing and doing well inspired her. When she got back home, the new ball her family purchased for her was tried out.
"She threw nine practice games with it at Doverama yesterday and two of them were a 232 and 230, the highest games she has ever thrown, if you count practice."
Proof Ticknor is just getting the ball rolling.

 AMERICAN CORNER — One game.That was the grand sum total of victories for Hurlock during the Colonel Basketball Association Summer League's six-game regular season.
Hurlock earned a pair of postseason victories though, and narrowly missed a third Wednesday night, before Enoch Dupri's free throw with 1.3 seconds remaining lifted Seaford (Delaware) to a 48-47 victory in the league championship at Colonel Richardson High's Merrill Morgan Gymnasium.
"We've come a long way this summer," said Hurlock head coach John Ridenour, an assistant for North Dorchester High's varsity. "I mean we won one game before the playoffs started and we came out and won two, and took Seaford to the brink. It would have been nice."
Like Stevensville and Saints Peter and Paul, Hurlock finished the regular season 1-5, but earned the fifth seed for the playoffs based on its margin of victory in its one win. Hurlock knocked off No. 4 seed Ridgely on Monday, then upset unbeaten top-seed and defending league champion Federalsburg, 47-38, in Wednesday's first semifinal.
Seaford reached the final via its 54-34 win over third-seeded Centreville in the second semifinal. The Blue Jays looked ready to turn the title game into a waltz, building a 17-7 lead after the first quarter, and stretching that edge to 39-25 midway through the third.
But Hurlock steadily began whittling its deficit, starting with Tajir Pritchett's bucket with 4:30 left in the third. Wyatt Barone (12 points), who plays for St. Michaels High, scored on a follow. Tyrone Smith (game-high 16 points) scored on a drive then hit 3 of 4 foul shots, capping a 9-0 quarter-closing run that pulled Hurlock within 39-34 heading into the fourth.
"To be honest, we came in here with the expectation of playing Colonel Richardson (Federalsburg) in the championship game," Seaford head coach Vince Evans II said. "I think once we realized it wasn't them, I don't think we played up to our expectations and kind of went through the motions. If we do that during the (high school) season that's going to cost us."
It almost cost Seaford on this night.
Smith sank a free throw and scored on a finger roll, trimming Seaford's lead to 39-37 early in the fourth. Seaford's Taj Bacon hit a 3-pointer. But Barone, who seemingly got stronger and stronger on both the offensive and defensive boards as the game progressed, scored inside, getting Hurlock within 42-39 with 7 minutes left.
Brendan West converted a Vince Evans feed to nudge Seaford's lead to 44-39. Again Barone, who netted eight fourth-quarter points, responded inside. Sammy Robinson's follow restored the Blue Jays' five-point lead at 46-41 with 2:40 left. Barone made a put-back and Smith scored on a drive, drawing Hurlock within 46-45 with 2 minutes to play.
"The guys just fought," Ridenour said. "They played hard and that's all I asked of them is give it their all."
Ridenour also acknowledged having played the first semifinal allowed his players to rest while Seaford started its second game about 10 minutes after its semifinal victory.
"We got a break in between games," Ridenour said. "To be honest I think it helps sometimes having a smaller seven; seven, eight guys. It's easier to maneuver and you can see what rotations are working a little better."
Dupri (team-high 12 points) converted one of two from the foul line for a 47-45 Seaford lead with 56 seconds left. Barone's turnaround jumper tied it at 47-all with 37.3 seconds to go. Seaford called timeout with 15.6 seconds left. Dupri was fouled in the chaotic closing seconds and hit the first of two free-throw attempts with 1.3 seconds left.
Confusion about how much time was left ensued and officials decided 2 seconds should be put on the clock. But Jayden Turner's three-quarter court desperation heave hit a ceiling beam, ending the game.
"Credit to them because they played hard," coach Evans said of Hurlock. "They struggled throughout the league, but hats off to North Dorchester for playing hard, for knocking off Colonel. And they should have beat us. They played a lot harder than we did."

 HURLOCK — Austin Frank didn't know how many pitches he threw.And after getting buried under an avalanche of red, white and blue-clad teammates after a second nine-inning victory, he may have temporarily forgotten where he was — cloud nine or the infield at the American Legion baseball field in Hurlock.
What Frank did know was where he and his teammates were headed this Friday afternoon.
"We're going to Hanover. We're going to Joe Cannon Stadium," Frank said of this year's American Legion state baseball tournament site.
Frank pitched 7 2/3 innings of shutout baseball over two games, then stroked a two-out single to score Hayden Diefenderfer with the winning run in the bottom of the ninth inning Tuesday night, giving Caroline Post 29 a 3-2 victory over Talbot Post 70 and a sweep of the best-of-three Eastern Shore North Division playoff series.
Winners of five straight division titles, Caroline is slated to play Eastern Shore South Division champion Ocean City at 4 p.m. Friday in the first round of the state tournament.
"Austin loves baseball," said Caroline first-year manager Travis Breeding. "He knows the game inside and out. You can always count on him to come through and rise to the situation."
Boy, did Frank rise to the situation.
Game 1, which was suspended last Thursday with the score tied 4-4 after seven innings, remained knotted until the top of the ninth. Caroline's Gavin Whitby hit a leadoff single to center field, moved to second on an error, and scored when Wes Thomas ripped a double to left field off Talbot's Couper Barletta for a 5-4 lead.
Frank, who retired Post 70 in order in the eighth, struck out the side in the ninth to seal the 5-4 Game 1 victory.
Frank remained on the mound to start the second game, which became a scoreless pitcher's duel between Post 29's right-hander and Talbot lefty Cullen Murphy. Frank surrendered no runs, three hits, three walks and struck out seven over 5 2/3 scoreless innings before reaching his pitch limit with two outs in the sixth.
"I had most of my stuff with me today," Frank said of his fastball, slider and change-up. "They all looked good. They all felt great. I could just locate really well. I felt like I could put the ball where I wanted it."
"He's a tough, tough pitcher," Talbot manager Albert Pritchett said of Frank.
Murphy was equally tough, yielding no runs, two hits, six walks and striking out eight over 5 2/3 innings.
"Cullen did a great job of holding us in it," said Pritchett, whose southpaw reached his limit after fanning the first two batters in the sixth.
Talbot broke the scoreless stalemate in the top of the eighth.
Anthony Massaro lined a leadoff single to center off Caroline reliever Chase Hitchens. Jesus Crespo singled through the right side, pushing Massaro to third. Pearson Greenwood then skied a single down the right-field line, scoring Massaro for a 1-0 lead. Ethan Royer followed, doubling into the right-center field gap to plate Crespo for a 2-0 Post 70 lead.
Talbot (5-3-1) appeared on the verge of widening its lead when Jordan Langrell walked, loading the bases. Gavin Murphy singled into shallow left, but Frank, now playing left field, fired a strike to the plate to get the force on Talbot's pinch-runner for the inning's first out. Hitchens then induced an inning-ending double play, keeping Caroline's deficit at 2-0.
Still, Post 70 looked ready to force a Game 3 — which was slated to be played at the conclusion of Game 2 — as reliever Nathan Spurry retired the first two batters of the eighth. But Derrick Mitchell reached on an infield single. Whitby walked. David Saathoff lined a sharp single to left, loading the bases. Johnny Radcliff then smacked a 2-2 delivery into center field, plating Mitchell and Whitby for a 2-2 tie. Spurry intentionally walked Kenton Robbins to reload the bases in hopes of a force at any base, before notching an inning-ending strikeout.
Hitchens set Post 70 down in order in the top of the ninth.
Colton Maans began Caroline's game-winning rally in the ninth, reaching on a one-out infield single with no one covering first base. Diefenderfer came on to pinch run, was balked to second base and advanced to third on Trent Breeding's groundout to second. Frank followed, hitting a 1-2 pitch up the middle to score Diefender with the winning run.
"He went first-pitch slider and then went slider again," Frank said of Spurry. "Then he went fastball so I knew he was going to come back to it. I was sitting slider and he threw it and I got a good swing on it."
Frank touched first base, raised both arms to his sides in celebration. Mitchell reached Caroline's hero first, quickly hoisting him upward before a steady wave of teammates sent both tumbling to the ground.
"Big shoes to fill definitely with the success the program had had," Travis Breeding said of succeeding former skipper Neil Lambert. "They really are a good group of guys. You saw how they clawed and fought back. I was like, 'Here we go. We're going to be here until the lights go off, trying to get another game in to be the decider.' They just battled back. I can't say enough about their fortitude and how they stayed in the ballgame when they could have got down. They're just determined. They were determined to win."

title: Scheffler storms into lead
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Scheffler storms into lead

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News

 PORTRUSH, Northern Ireland — The rain pounded Royal Portrush right when Scottie Scheffler poured in a birdie putt on his first hole Friday in the British Open. No matter. Nothing stopped the world's No. 1 player on his way to a 7-under 64 to build a one-shot lead going into the weekend.Scheffler made eight birdies on another wild afternoon of weather at Royal Portrush, and his 15-foot birdie attempt on the 18th stopped inches short for another.
The result was a one-shot lead over former U.S. Open champion Matt Fitzpatrick, who made four straight birdies to start the back nine until he cooled on the home stretch and had to settle for a 66.
The rain was heavy at times but never lasted long. The wind was breezy but never at strength that can cause fits. The scoring was lower, nearly two shots easier than the opening round.
Except for a few chasers, Scheffler made it look like it wasn't enough.
He was at 10-under 132 as he chases the third leg of the career Grand Slam, having won the PGA Championship by five shots in May.
Brian Harman got the best of the weather — surprising sunshine — and took dead aim in his hunt for another claret jug. Harman played bogey-free for a 64 that left him only two shots behind, along with Li Haotong of China, who had a 67.
Everyone else was five shots behind or more.
That includes Rory McIlroy, who went around Royal Portrush in his native Northern Ireland with plenty of cheers but only a few roars. McIlroy had a 69 but lost a lot of ground because of Scheffler, Fitzpatrick and Harman.
He started the second round just three shots behind. He goes into the weekend seven shots behind the top-ranked player in the world.
Fitzpatrick was at his lowest point just four months ago when he changed his caddie and coach and began pulling himself up. And now he takes that into the weekend against Scheffler.
"He's going to have the expectation to go out and dominate. He's an exceptional player. He's world No. 1, and we're seeing Tiger-like stuff," Fitzpatrick said. "I think the pressure is for him to win the golf tournament. For me, obviously I hope I'm going to have some more home support than him, but it's an exciting position for me to be in given where I was earlier this year."
Fitzpatrick was rolling along until a pair of short putts he missed, from 5 feet for par on the 14th and from 3 feet for birdie on the 17th. Even so, he holed a 25-foot par putt on the final hole and assured him being in the last group at 9-under 133.
Scheffler was sharp from the start. He hit eight of the 14 fairways — compared with three in the opening round — though his misses never left him too badly out of position. But he is seeing the breaks on smoother Portrush greens, and he looks confident as ever.
None of his eight birdies were closer than 7 feet. Five of them were in the 10-foot range and then he threw in a 35-foot birdie on the sixth. His lone bogey came on a drive into deep grass on the 11th that kept him from reaching the green.
The statistics led to a shrug.
"Overall, I'm hitting the ball solid," Scheffler said. "The tournament is only halfway done. I got off to a good start."
Harman was called the "Butcher of Hoylake" when he won the claret jug at Royal Liverpool two years ago because the British press was fascinated by the Georgia native's love for hunting. Now it's about his golf, and it was superb.
Harman played bogey-free, only once having to stress for par as Royal Portrush allowed for some good scoring in weather that again did not live up to its expectation.
Not that anyone was complaining. Temperatures were warm, at least by Irish standards. The breeze was noticeable without being overly punishing.
"They're very different golf courses, but the golf is similar," Harman said. "You've got to be able to flight your golf ball. You've got to know how far everything's going. Then you can't get frustrated. You're going to end up in funny spots where it doesn't seem fair, and you just have to kind of outlast that stuff."
The group at 5-under 137 included Harris English (70), Harman's former teammate at Georgia; Tyrrell Hatton of England (69) and Chris Gotterup (65), who wasn't even planning to be at Royal Portrush until winning the Scottish Open last week.
Also still around is Bryson DeChambeau, who made a 13-shot improvement from the first round with a 65. Still, he was 11 shots behind.
McIlroy wasn't at his best in the opening round and was pleased to be only three behind. Now he has a real mountain to climb. But at least he's still playing, unlike in 2019 at Royal Portrush when he shot 79 and then had a terrific rally only to miss the cut by one shot.
"I didn't have this opportunity six years ago, so to play an extra two days in this atmosphere in front of these crowds, I'm very excited for that," McIlroy said. "I feel like my game's definitely good enough to make a run."
That was before Scheffler began to run away from so many except a small collection of challengers. But this is links golf. And this is the Emerald Isle, where the weather seems to have a mind of its own.
Still, Scheffler has gone 10 tournaments without finishing out of the top 10 and would appear to present a challenge every bit as daunting as Royal Portrush.

Federalsburg (6-0) will be the No. 1 seed and have a first-round bye for next week's playoffs.
"They're playing great," Hammond said of his defending league champions, who were led by Ja'Zir Dickerson's game-high 34 points. "We're working on defense, having better ball movement, and having fun."
Makiah Batson (26 points) drilled a 3-pointer and scored a layup, watched Robbie Cunningham drain a three-ball, then splashed another trey for a quick 11-0 Federalsburg lead that ballooned to 21-0. Centreville (4-2), which entered the game tied for second place with Seaford, finally got on the board with 1 minute, 49 seconds remaining in the first quarter, when Jared Robinson connected on a 3-pointer.
Federalsburg, which is made up mostly of Colonel Richardson High players, carried a 24-6 lead into the second quarter. Batson canned a 3-pointer and scored a pair of layups to restore Federalsburg's 21-point cushion at 31-10 with 7 minutes left in the first half.
DeRodney Smith (team-high 21 points) sandwiched a pair of 3-pointers around a follow-shot that helped pull Centreville within 35-20 with under a minute left in the first half.
"You're going to have little mess-ups during the game," Hammond said. "But if you start out hot, end off hot, you're going to come out with a great game."

title: Ravens' Hamilton voted NFL' s top safety

Ravens' Hamilton voted NFL' s top safety

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Kyle Hamilton has quickly proved that he can be a jack of all trades on Baltimore's stellar defense, thriving in the slot, the box or as a deep safety.But it was the decision to move Hamilton to free safety midway through last season that helped eliminate the big plays and boost the Ravens' defense.
Hamilton's talent and versatility helped him earn the honor of being voted the top safety in the league by The Associated Press.
A panel of eight AP Pro Football Writers ranked the top five players at safety, basing selections on current status entering the 2025 season. First-place votes were worth 10 points. Second- through fifth-place votes were worth 5, 3, 2 and 1 points.
Hamilton got five first place-votes, one second and one third to claim the top spot. Detroit's Kerby Joseph got the other three first-place votes and finished second.
Green Bay's Xavier McKinney, Detroit's Brian Branch and Derwin James of the Los Angeles Chargers rounded out the top five.
Atlanta's Jessie Bates, Tampa Bay's Antoine Winfield Jr., Miami's Minkah Fitzpatrick, Denver's Brandon Jones, Arizona's Budda Baker and Houston's C.J. Gardner-Johnson also received votes.
1. KYLE HAMILTON, Baltimore Ravens
Hamilton has been the most important piece on Baltimore's defense thanks in large part to his versatility. He has the ability to stop the run, excel against the pass and rush the quarterback and was voted a first-team All-Pro in 2023 and second-teamer last season. Hamilton played the majority of his snaps starting in Week 11 last season as a free safety and the Ravens went from allowing 4.7 pass plays of at least 20 yards per game to 1.6 after the switch.
2. KERBY JOSEPH, Detroit Lions
Joseph emerged as a big-time playmaker in his third season, leading the NFL with nine interceptions to earn first-team All-Pro honors. His 17 career interceptions are the most for any safety in his first three seasons since Hall of Famer Ed Reed had 21.
3. XAVIER MCKINNEY, Green Bay Packers
McKinney made a major impact on Green Bay's defense in his first season after signing with the Packers as a free agent. He was at his best in pass coverage as a deep safety. McKinney had eight interceptions last season and allowed a 56.4 passer rating when targeted in coverage, according to Pro Football Focus.
4. BRIAN BRANCH, Detroit Lions
Branch has become an immediate impact player on Detroit's defense since being drafted in the second round in 2023. He led all safeties with 16 passes defensed last season and was tied for third with eight tackles for loss as he performed at a high level both in the run and pass game.
5. DERWIN JAMES, Los Angeles Chargers
James bounced back from a down 2023 season to earn second-team All-Pro honors in his first season in coordinator Jesse Minter's defense. James is one of the most versatile safeties, getting extensive time working in the slot, as a box safety, a deep safety and even as a pass rusher, where he had the second-most pressures of any safety last season.

St. Michaels' Sherwood, Easton's Webb set to play in Robinson all-star game

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Neither has chased the dream of playing major league baseball."I've always loved the game of baseball," St. Michaels High graduate Will Sherwood said. "But I never thought of it as like big leagues. Maybe when I was real, real young. But I've always just loved to play. As long as I'm out there I don't really care what happens."
Easton High grad Kayden Webb echoed Sherwood's sentiment.
"It wasn't really something that I was trying to pursue," Webb said of a potential professional career. "Never really thought about that. I just kind of like playing the game of baseball."
Sherwood and Webb will be playing again this Sunday — only this time in a big-league park — as members of the South team in the annual Brooks Robinson High School All Star Game at Oriole Park at Camden Yards in Baltimore. The game is scheduled to start after Sunday's Orioles-Miami Marlins game.
"Awesome. Never thought I'd be playing there," said Sherwood, whose older brother Josh played in the 2022 all-star game. "Just happy to get the opportunity to play in a game like this."
"Just excited," said Webb, the first Easton player chosen for the team since 2021, when Max Vener was selected as an alternate. "I just feel like I'll let it all in when I get there."
Sherwood and Webb each played in the Maryland State Association of Baseball Coaches' Prospects Game as freshmen, which is factored in as part of the selection process for the Brooks Robinson game. Both played in the MSABC Futures Game as sophomores. Webb played in the Futures Game again last year, while Sherwood played in the Classic Game.
This year's MSABC Classic game, which offered players another chance to showcase their talents, was rained out. That left Sherwood and Webb uncertain if they would be selected, and somewhat surprised when they learned they had made the team.
"I thought about it my freshman year, just kind of working towards it," Webb said of possibly being picked for the Robinson game. "It was pretty cool to see that happen."
"I knew there was a chance, but I wasn't sure because of the people picking the team," Sherwood added.
Sherwood, who pitched and played right field, led St. Michaels to a 16-6 record this season and a 10th appearance in the Class 1A state championship, where the Saints lost 6-2 to Allegany. The right-hander was 6-2 and led the North Bayside in wins and innings pitched (52). His 1.48 earned-run average was second only to Colonel Richardson senior standout Jordan Regulski (1.42), who is headed to Wake Forest University. Sherwood finished the year with four complete games, 43 strikeouts and 17 walks.
"If you took him off our team, we'd probably lose five or six more ballgames," St. Michaels head coach Brian Femi said of Sherwood. "It's not a question in my mind. He pitched every big game we had. And then he hits."
Sherwood, who is headed to Chesapeake College to play, batted .386, leading St. Michaels in hits (27), RBIs (25) and home runs (two). He also had six doubles, a triple, 21 runs scored, and a .522 on-base percentage.
"He basically, and I haven't had a kid do this in a long time, he put our team on his back," Femi said. "He was the most unbelievable leader. You just can't measure it. He took all the young kids, he made them feel welcomed. Our team chemistry was as good as it was when Adam (Parks) and those guys were there (in 2010-11). You had that kind of leadership. Not many other coaches would have seen the leadership that he had because they weren't present."
One year after struggling with an injury to his right arm, Webb emerged as Easton's ace, posting a 4-2 mark with a 2.944 ERA, 28 strikeouts and 20 walks. When he wasn't on the mound, Webb was in center field and finished the season batting over .400 with 20 hits, two doubles, three triples, 12 RBIs, 26 runs, and a .587 OBP.
"He's worked hard his four years," Easton head coach Albert Pritchett said of Webb, who is playing for the Baltimore Chop of the Maryland Collegiate Baseball League this summer before heading to Salisbury University to play. "He showed up every day, every practice. I think over the four years he developed into more of a leader by example, as well as his verbal contributions. He was just a pleasure to watch develop. Strong player. Very athletic. Left us as an even better player. Kind of kid you want to play with. Calm on the outside, fire on the inside. Made every team he was on better."
Sherwood and Webb are listed as outfielders, but could possibly pitch Sunday.
Femi will be on the South coaching staff Sunday. Washington High's Dawson Daniels also made the South team, giving the Bayside Conference three players on the roster.

title: Little consensus on Nats' top pick
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Little consensus on Nats' top pick

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 The Washington Nationals are at a pivotal point in their rebuild to relevance, owning the No. 1 overall pick in Major League Baseball's amateur draft that begins on Sunday night in Atlanta.There are multiple intriguing prospects they can choose from, including prep shortstop Ethan Holliday, the son of seven-time All-Star Matt Holliday and brother of Jackson Holliday, the No. 1 overall pick in 2022 and is now in the majors with the Baltimore Orioles.
Washington this week fired longtime general manager Mike Rizzo and manager Dave Martinez.
Bold choice.
The Nats' head-scratching move — more for the timing than the actual decision — injected another layer of uncertainty to a draft that might be one of the most unpredictable in recent years. The first three rounds of the 20-round draft will take place on Sunday with the rest of the selections on Monday.
Washington promoted Mike DeBartolo to interim GM and he'll supervise the team's selections. He was previously the team's assistant general manager and has been with the franchise since 2012.
DeBartolo said he'll lean on the evaluations of the team's scouting department but also has his own opinions about the process and will be the decision maker. Money will also be a factor, as teams have to work within their bonus pool.
The Orioles are at the high end this year with more than $19 million to spend. The Yankees — who don't pick until No. 39 — are at the bottom with roughly $5.3 million.
"They've been working hard for this moment, almost even before the last draft ended," DeBartolo said. "So, I'll bring my own voice to that process, and I'll work collaboratively with them, and take what they have to say and ultimately be responsible for making the picks."
There is little consensus about whom the Nats might select at No. 1, though some of the top prospects are a pair of left-handed pitchers — LSU's Kade Anderson and Tennessee's Liam Doyle — along with Oregon State shortstop Aiva Arquette and prep shortstops Holliday and Eli Willits.
"There are several really talented players that are going to be in the mix for us," DeBartolo said. "We have to decide how to strategize with our bonus pool money and what the player bonus pool demands are and run through all those scenarios over the coming days."
After the Nationals, the Los Angeles Angels have the No. 2 selection. The Seattle Mariners, Colorado Rockies and St. Louis Cardinals round out the top five.
LEFTIES LEAD PACKSeveral of the top prospects are left-handed college pitchers, including Anderson, Doyle and Florida State's Jamie Arnold.
Anderson helped LSU win the College World Series title last month, throwing a complete-game shutout in Game 1 of the championship series. He finished 12-1 with a 3.18 ERA with 180 strikeouts in 119 innings.
Anderson had Tommy John surgery in high school.
Doyle rocketed up mock drafts with a terrific season for the Vols, finishing 10-4 with a 3.20 ERA and 162 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings. Arnold was a breakout star for Florida State in 2024 before regressing a bit last season, but he still finished with 8-2 with a 2.98 ERA and 119 strikeouts.
"Obviously, college left-handers are kind of a premium right now," Mariners vice president of amateur scouting Scott Hunter said. "There's a few of those at the high end of the draft."
CORONA STARSCorona High School — about 45 miles from Los Angeles — could have three players drafted in the first round.
The prep powerhouse is led by right-handed pitcher Seth Hernandez, regarded as a potential top five pick. Shortstop Billy Carlson is also expected to be selected early in the first round.
Third baseman Brady Ebel isn't quite as highly-regarded — he's the No. 64 prospect according to MLB.com — but there's potential that he could still sneak into the opening round.
A fourth Corona player, Ethin Bingaman, is a two-way player committed to Auburn but could be drafted in the top five rounds.

Easton's Hershey named player of the year; St. Michaels Miller selected coach of the year
