 Easton High's Jake Hershey wanted another shot at the champ."Yes. He felt like there was a little unfinished business, and he knew he wanted to get back and have another chance at the same young man," Warrior boys head tennis coach Aaron Hutt said.
Hershey came within a win of becoming the first boys singles player to win a state title in school — and North Bayside — history a year ago, only to be denied by Poolesville's Andy Wu in the Class 2A final.
Carrying an 18-0 record into this year's state tournament, Hershey was on course for a rematch with Wu. That second chance was foiled though, when Hereford's Harry Smith defeated Hershey, 7-5, 6-2 in the semifinals.
With his hopes for a rematch and a state title gone, the recently-graduated Hershey could have easily packed his bag and made the long, slow drive back from the Wilde Lake Tennis Club in Columbia to Easton in heavy Memorial Day weekend traffic. Instead, the senior fell back on the family, friends and teammates that watched him play May 23.
"I owe a lot of that to my family and the people I was there with; my teammates," Hershey said of moving forward. "(Teammate) Clay Nagle, similar situation happened to him and his partner, Parker Jimenez (who lost in the mixed doubles semifinals). We went back (to the hotel), had a nice relaxing night. I think that's where the team aspect comes into it in moments like that, where they help you get yourself together when you might not be exactly where you want to be mentally."
Hershey returned the following day and defeated C. Milton Wright's Xavier Moaddel, 6-0, 6-4 in the third-place match, capping a 20-1 season in singles play that earned him the North Bayside's boys tennis player of the year as voted on by the division's coaches.
Nagle and Jimenez also rebounded from their semifinal loss, defeating Wilde Lake's Jakob Bluemner and Jillian Davis, 6-0, 6-0 in the third-place match in 2A mixed doubles.
"There's an old saying: You can let it go to your heart for a moment, but you can't let it go to your head," Hutt said of the disappointment that comes from a loss. "And he was able to compartmentalize that loss, granted being very upset. But after a few hours, he put it together and said, 'OK, next challenge.' It's a testament not just to his resilience, but the experience he's gotten from traveling and playing some pretty high-level tennis."
That experience helped Hershey go undefeated during the regular season in singles, compile a 14-1 record in doubles, and win a third straight Class 2A East Region II singles title. And though he did not get a second crack at Wu — who went on to win a third straight 2A state title — Hershey showed growth through the season.
"I think he matured, and his ability to not be his own worst enemy was apparent," Hutt said of Hershey, who was 57-2 over four years in the regular season, and intends to continue playing at Catholic University. "Last year, and past years, something might not go quite right and he internalized it automatically, forgetting that the other person has something to do with it as well. And that's kind of what greatness does. It looks at what it needs to do initially, and then it realizes, it's not just what I need to do, it's what I need to do to stop them as well. He got very good at that. Not only that, but being able to play every game as its own little match. He only lost a handful of games let alone sets."
St. Michaels' boys team didn't lose a match this season until the Bayside Conference championship, where it fell 4-3 to Stephen Decatur. But that was the lone blemish on a season of firsts for St. Michaels tennis, earning 11-year head coach Jordan Miller the North Bayside boys coach of the year.
"I knew we were going to be a very strong team," Miller said. "I worked with throughout the year most of the players that we see. So I know what we have. And I also know what everybody else has. I knew our guys were putting in a lot of work. And that was going to be very helpful."
One year after falling shy of the division via a 4-3 loss against North Caroline, St. Michaels dominated its North competition with an 18-1 overall record, winning 14 matches by 7-0 scores, and three others by 6-1 margins. The Saints not only won their first division title and reached the conference championship for the first time, they earned a fourth consecutive 1A East Region I crown.
St. Michaels wasn't quite finished though.
Lexi Rockwell and Tom Weller teamed to win the school's first state tennis championship, when they won the 1A mixed doubles crown. That effort, coupled with Sean Kline and Miles Fox finishing third in boys doubles, and Tess Weller placing fourth in girls singles, helped the Saints take runner-up honors in the 1A team competition at states — another program first — by just one point.
"It was definitely a good feeling," Miller said.
It may also prove to be good motivation for next season.
"I talked with my assistant (Casey Capute)," Miller said. "We didn't like coming home with the second-place trophy as a team for states. And we didn't like coming home with a second-place (at Baysides). I hate for us to be, 'OK, we got a state championship and we're happy with that.'
"Prior to coming back (as head coach), I never knew what we were capable of," added Miller, a St. Michaels graduate. "But the more I coached, the more I saw opportunities for us, if we could just get a few kids to really buy in. And now we've got quite a few more than a few kids that have bought in. And I think we're going to be able to hopefully maintain that for many years to come.
Here's a look at the rest of the this year's teams
FIRST TEAMSebastian Cousineau, So., Kent County
Became the first in school history to reach a state championship, where he lost in the 1A final to Boonsboro senior Hunter Liao, who became the state's first four-time state champion in boys singles. Cousineau was 13-2 in singles — his only other loss coming against Easton's Hershey — and 6-4 in doubles. The sophomore beat Colonel Richardson's Jeffrey Lin, 6-2, 6-4 to win 1A East I title.
Miles Fox, Jr., St. Michaels
Fox was 14-2 in singles, which included a win against Decatur at Baysides. Teamed with Sean Kline in doubles, posting a 16-0 conference record, and a 21-1 overall mark. The tandem beat Decatur at Bayside, won the 1A East I boys doubles title with a 6-0, 6-0 sweep of Perryville's Holden Coe and Tyler Loss, and reached the state semifinals. Defeated Southern Garrett's Ben Nazelrod and Shane Sisler, 6-1, 6-2 in consolation final.

Kline posted a 13-3 singles mark during the regular season, losing only to Hershey, Cousineau and Queen Anne's County's Tyler Olah — all first-team all-North picks.

title: Rockwell, Fisher net North's top honors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Rockwell, Fisher net North's top honors

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Lexi Rockwell had always set goals."But I feel like she didn't realize how high she could set them early on," St. Michaels High head tennis coach Jordan Miller said of his No. 1 girls player. "And once she did it felt like she could do anything."
Well, the senior raised the bar higher than ever before this spring, wanting to earn player-of-the-year honors and win a state championship.
She did both.
Rockwell went undefeated in singles play, then slapped an exclamation point on her season by teaming with Tom Weller to win the Class 1A state title in mixed doubles, giving St. Michaels its first state tennis crown en route to earning the All-North Bayside Girls Player of the Year, as selected by the division coaches.
"She wanted to be player of the year and she wanted to win a state title," Miller said. "And she accomplished all those things by determination and hard work. She put in the hours, doing some extra running before and after practice, to make sure she was in good physical condition."
Rockwell also put a lot of time in playing against members of the Saints' boys team to give her more of a challenge during the year. The results were a 15-0 singles record and a 12-3 slate in doubles.
Her and Weller went 3-0 to win the Class 1A East Region I mixed doubles title, leading St. Michaels to a fourth straight regional team title. Rockwell and Weller then went 3-0 at states, which included a 6-1, 6-2 victory over Mountain Ridge's Marissa Greg and Aiden Pirolozzi in the final, earning the Saints' their first state crown of any sort in tennis and a runner-up finish in the team standings.
"She's very much an all-around player," Miller said of Rockwell, who finished the season 33-3. "One of the stronger girls' serves in the Bayside (Conference) for sure. Rock-steady from the baseline. Just never missed. Hit with good pace and depth. And she had a game plan that she executed every single time. It was start to the backhand, open up the court, and then hit the opposite way. And it worked very, very well."
Miller thought that game plan was one of the key pieces that gave Rockwell an added edge this season.
"She's been hitting a good ball since she was a freshman," Miller said. "Last year she did have a lot of good results," (which included reaching the 1A state girls doubles final with Lila Jones). "But I felt like she didn't really have her game plan. This year when she went out there, she knew what she was going to do. It didn't matter what the other person did across the net."
Named the North Bayside Coach of the Year, Queen Anne's County head coach Dee Fisher's objective for the season was vastly different than Rockwell's.
"My goal going into the season was to play 10 girls at every match, and to get all of my 28 players match time," Fisher said. "Twenty-five people actually played against another school, (some in) exhibition matches. And there was at least six or seven times where we had 10 different girls playing at a varsity match. That was my goal."
The Lions were also playing with a different label than any Fisher-led team had worn in his 25 seasons as head coach — defending Bayside champion.
"Nothing changed," Fisher said. "We just went out and they played. I always talk with my captains about what our lineup should look like because a lot of teams only play six people. They have their strongest four, they play doubles and singles, and then that's it. But a lot of times we change our lineup up. So we may have our top four players just play singles, and then everybody else play doubles. Or our top four play doubles and people play singles. It was more of a team effort."
No matter what the lineup, the Lions won, going 18-0 to win their second consecutive division and conference titles, and pushing their record to 35-1 over the past two seasons.
Fisher, who has forever preached to his players, "Just have fun and play," admitted he didn't feel any pressure this season until the tiebreaker of the Class 2A state girls doubles final, when sisters Lucy and Meg Taylor earned a 3-6, 6-3, 11-9 victory over Poolesville's Kyra McGlinchey and Pranahitha Kanuparthi, giving Queen Anne's its first-ever state title.
"This year we had so many people coming back, and I knew we were going to go all the way," Fisher said of winning the conference title. "It was never a question if we were able to win every match because I know how strong the girls were, and how great leaders they are."
Here's a look at the rest of this year's all-North Bayside teams:
First Team
Lucy Taylor, Sr., Queen Anne's
Went 9-6 at No. 1 singles and joined younger sister Meg to go 11-2 in doubles. The Taylors gave Queen Anne's its first state tennis title, winning the 2A state girls doubles championship. That was the first state title in girls doubles for a Bayside team since Cambridge-South Dorchester's Heidi McWilliams and Abby Messick won their second straight in 1991, ending the conference's longest drought in the state's five brackets.
Meg Taylor, Jr., Queen Anne's
The other half of Lions state doubles championship tandem, Meg compiled a 9-5 mark at No. 2 singles before going on to make school history with Lucy.
Maddie Tobat, Sr., North Dorchester
The school's valedictorian who also played lacrosse, Maddie went 14-1 in singles and doubles. Her and twin sister Jules won the Class 1A East Region II girls doubles championship, and came within a win of giving the Eagles their first state tennis title, falling in the 1A finals.

North Dorchester's salutorian, Jules also played lacrosse and joined her sister to win the regional title in girls doubles before reaching the 1A state finals. Finished the year 14-1 in singles, 13-2 in doubles.

 Cambridge is known for its triathlons. On the Fourth of July, children as young as 6 years old participated in their own triathlon, the Gerry Boye Firecracker Kids Triathlon.The event saw 111 children from 6 to 15 years old competing in swimming, cycling and running, just like in the full marathon. For the Firecracker, the distances were greatly pared down for the young athletes who competed in five groups based on their age.
The swim was done in the YMCA pool with 6 and year old swimming 25 yards, the length of the pool; 8 and 9 year olds swimming 50 yards; 10 and 11 year old swimming 100 yards; 12 and 13 year olds swimming 150 yards; and 14 and 15 year old swimming eight lengths of the pool, 200 yards.
All athletes competed in a 2-mile bike ride that also allows for training wheels the youngest competitors. The triathlon capped off with a run of 1 kilometer for 6 to 10 year olds and a full mile for the older competitors.
There were 35 volunteers who helped set up the course, provide traffic control and assist the young athletes in each event.
"It truly takes a village to make it happen each year, and we are deeply grateful to the dedicated volunteers who make it possible," race director Lynn Stewart said.
Proceeds from the event go to scholarships for graduating high school students. This year scholarships were awarded to:
Kevin Banda-Perez, North Dorchester High School.Rodney Harris, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.Isabelle Hughes, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.Camryn Russum, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.
According to Stewart, the Gerry Boyle Firecracker Kids' Triathlon was launched in 2012 by Cambridge Multi-Sport to give local children a fun, confidence-building introduction to the sport. The late Gerry Boyle — who served as race director for both Ironman 70.3 Eagleman and Ironman Maryland and was instrumental in bringing races to Cambridge in 2014 — was a passionate supporter of the Firecracker.
As a comparison to the Firecracker triathlon, the Ironman covers 140.6 miles, comprising a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride and a 26.2-mile run.
Since his death in 2019, the Firecracker race has carried Boyle's name and honors his legacy, she said.

title: Easton's cradle king stood for more than wins and losses
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton's cradle king stood for more than wins and losses

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1153
 Words 

 Read News Document

 He never won a title or set any records. And not once in three seasons on Easton High's wrestling team did he qualify for the regional or state tournament.But then wins and losses weren't what made Darren Foxwell stand out.
"The thing with Darren is he's such a unique person," Adonis Schmitt, a wrestling teammate, said of Foxwell, who died Wednesday, June 18, from injuries sustained in a single-car accident the day before.
That certainly fit the way Foxwell decided to briefly quit the wrestling team early this past season.
Easton's starter at 167 pounds, Foxwell didn't just stop coming to practice without explanation. He didn't try dodging head coach Jason Biringer or attempt to find a new way to class in an effort to avoid passing Biringer's room like he had every morning.
Instead, the 18-year-old sought out Biringer during his planning period in the teacher's lounge. He told his coach face to face he just couldn't do it anymore, and just wanted to enjoy his senior year.
Before leaving the lounge, Foxwell handed Biringer six envelopes. One was for Biringer. The other five were for Easton's assistant coaches. Each envelope contained a hand-written letter from Foxwell thanking Biringer and assistants Steve Culver, James Gardner, Chris Danels, Jason Perez and Josh Valdez for all they had done for him.
"It caught me off guard," Biringer said. "I was shocked when he gave it to me. Then I read it, and I was like, 'Oh my God. What does that tell us about him? What an outstanding kid.' He wrote how much I helped him and how much of an impact I had on him. A lot of times kids just ghost and disappear. You see them in the hall and they're like, oh, they don't want to confront you."
Not Foxwell. Maybe that's why a few days later, Biringer sought out Foxwell and pulled him from class.
"I was like, 'Darren, what's going on? Just talk to me,'" Biringer recalled. "He said he didn't know if he had the passion for it anymore and it was a lot of work. I was like, 'Well, what got you into wrestling, or what did you like about it that made you come back for three years?' He said how he felt when he would go out on the mat and win, bonding with his brothers on the team. I said, 'You really want to give it up?' And he said, 'I don't know if I really do coach.'
"I said, 'Well, would you want to come back because I know we need a senior on our team with the affect you have. You're someone who's always trying hard and showing, not telling, kids what to do. They follow your lead.'"
Less than a week later, Foxwell was back on the team going through the grueling and exhaustive two-hour practices.
He was again having his face shoved into the mat, perhaps with the help of a forearm on the back of his head or neck. He was again running the risk of having his ears shaped into cauliflowers. He was again drilling, working on takedowns and escapes. He was again leaving the room drenched in sweat.
And he was again trying to help everyone around him.
"He could be having a bad day, a good day, it didn't matter," said Schmitt, who along with Foxwell accounted for the two seniors on the team. "He came to practice. He practiced hard. Those that he practiced with, and everybody around him, he lifted up. He made them better. No matter if it was a little bit, a lot, he made each and everyone of us better."
Biringer noticed and a little over a month after his return named Foxwell captain.
"He came back, and he was just so committed," Biringer said. "That was one of the things we pointed out at the awards night, just how he came back. He was just so motivated. He was just a positive presence honestly. The other wrestlers looked up to him. He has such a good, gentle demeanor that he was just very well liked. And kids loved to interact with him and that made him a good leader.
"Even off the mat," Biringer said. "Every morning he would walk past my room and he was like, 'Morning coach.' He just had one of those infectious smiles that your'e like, 'It's always good to see Darren.'"
Foxwell had earned the title of captain. He'd also earned a nickname along the way — cradle king, for his knack for using his 6-foot-3 frame to catch the neck of an opponent with one arm while wrapping the other arm behind the opponent's knees, creating a nice bundle.
"Just during practice, randomly, out of nowhere," said Schmitt, who along with teammates Esteban Velesquez and Wahaab Popal slapped Foxwell with the moniker. "He'd be in the craziest position and he'd just strike cradle. Like you'd be ready to go live (in practice). The next thing you know, you're on your back, pinned by cradle by the one and only cradle king."
Biringer laughed.
"He could be down 12-0 and then all of a sudden he would just lock a kid up and pin him," Biringer recalled. "And you'd just be shaking your head, saying, 'Oh, my gosh.' I remember James (Gardner) the first time this year we were in a match and he's getting beat. James is like, 'Don't worry.'"
Foxwell went 16-14 this season. After a loss, his unique side often resurfaced. The senior captain wouldn't storm off the mat in a rage or see if he could make history by trying to become the first to throw his headgear through a wall. Instead, Foxwell would check his disappointment, hit a quick reversal and return to encouraging his teammates in the matches that followed.
"He didn't like to lose," Schmitt said. "Over time it did get to him to a point where I know he was considering leaving. But he didn't leave. He stayed for the sake of the team. He stayed for the sake of the bond. He stayed for the sake of his peers and everybody that looked up to him."
Teammates weren't the only ones that looked up to Foxwell.
One of the requirements for Easton wrestlers is to help with the youth program that includes wrestlers ages 6 to 13. But Biringer noticed Foxwell lingering more and more after practice.
"I started noticing Darren hanging around.," Biringer said. "I was like, 'What are you doing?' He was like, 'I'm going to stick for these little guys.' And he stayed pretty much every youth practice just on his own volition, and he would work with these little kids.
"He wouldn't be able to stay all the time, and the kids were like, 'Is Darren going to be here?'" Biringer added. "I was like, 'No, he had to go home and do something.' And they were like, 'Awe, man.' So he obviously bonded with these little guys."
Those were the things that made Darren Foxwell stand out.

AN UNEXPECTED PATH ENDS

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 He'd played a handful of sports.There was T-ball, which naturally progressed into Easton Little League baseball. He was a member of the inaugural FC Tred Avon Rec Soccer League in 2016 and eventually went on to play two seasons with G.R. Cannon's Shore FC group. He even took a swing at tennis.
Once he was at Easton High though, wrestling became Darren Foxwell's primary sport.
Lacrosse?
Well, yeah he was raised in Talbot County, where many grew up with a rattle in one hand and a lacrosse stick in the other. And yes, he'd heard his father, Len Foxwell, former Easton Little League president, rant plenty of times about how the lacrosse fields at the North Easton Sports Complex were literally on higher ground than the baseball fields, which required so much more preparation after a good rain.
Darren came to lacrosse late. He made Easton's lacrosse team but lost his sophomore season after suffering a season-ending knee injury wrestling. He was back on varsity his junior and senior seasons, but he saw little playing time as a backup long-pole defenseman.
But in February of this year, lacrosse — college lacrosse that is — came to Darren via an out-of-the-blue phone call.
"I'll never forget this as long as I live," Len Foxwell said. "I was out having dinner with friends and Darren texted me and said, 'Hey, do you have a second? I want to run something by you regarding college.'
"I didn't know what he was talking about," Len continued. "I'm thinking, has he decided he doesn't want to go to Chesapeake (College) or Wor-Wic? Because that was the plan. He was going to go to community college and then eventually transfer probably to Salisbury."
Len pardoned himself from his dinner guests, stepped outside, took his son's call, and couldn't believe what he was hearing.
"'Dad, I have gotten an offer to play lacrosse at Bethany College,'" Darren told his father, adding he was going to receive financial assistance from the Division III school in West Virginia.
Len initially sensed a prank.
"I said, 'Darren, whatever number they called you on call it back and see who answers,'" Len said. "'Cause I thought it was a joke. Darren said, 'No. It's real. I've been talking to this coach (Bethany's Harold Palone III).'"
Len still wasn't convinced. Struggling to digest everything, he decided to make a direct call to Palone, who was entering just his second year as Bison head coach.
"We're talking, he's going a mile a minute, talking about his plans for Darren, 'How we need a long pole. This guy has left.' And I finally just said, 'Coach, just hold on for one second. I don't want this to be taken the wrong way, but why have you recruited Darren? He didn't get a lot of playing time,'" Len said.
What the senior defenseman did get though was a favorable report from longtime Easton head coach Dennis Keenan, who loved Darren's sense of humor.
"I think he was funnier than he actually thought he was," Keenan said. "The things he would say would just crack me up."
But Keenan also thought Darren had possibilities.
Coaching his final season, Keenan noted Foxwell's 6-foot-3 height. He added Darren had the wingspan of a pterodactyl and that he had gained upper body strength from being on Easton's wrestling team for three years. Keenan filed all that in the report he submitted on FieldLevel, a national athletic recruiting network that helps athletes and coaches find the right fit for potential prospects. A report that started Palone on the recruiting trail for Darren.
"'The only thing he lacks is experience and refinement,'" Foxwell recalled Palone saying during their phone conversation. "'And we can teach that. He's got the raw tools we need.'"
Darren committed with Bethany in March.
"He was getting better each day," Keenan said of Darren. "You could see flashes of brilliance. He was just a late bloomer; just a late starter. He had a bright future ahead of him."
Len felt the same way.
"This was a way to fuse those mental and physical attributes," Len said. "He had finally found his athletic path."
That path ended fatally just three weeks after Darren had graduated from Easton.
In the early morning of June 17, Darren sustained injuries as a passenger in a single-car crash outside Trappe. He was transported to Shock Trauma in Baltimore for treatment of life-threatening injuries. One day later, Darren Foxwell died. He was 18.
Len Foxwell last saw his son alive on Father's Day when they had lunch together. As he pulled up in front of Darren's home, Len noticed the corrugated sign out front that read, "Bethany Bound" and remembered an earlier conversation.
"I had been so focused on getting him to the next step, somehow getting him prepared for college," Len said. "And I said, 'Darren, these next four years at Bethany are going to be the best of your life.' And he said, 'These are the best years of my life right now at Easton High School. I have my friends here. I have it pretty good.' He cherished everything about his high school experience and being with his friends and brothers."
